title: Small Kakeya sets in F_3^6, F_3^7, F_3^8 and F_3^9
made_with: AI agents working in MV2's name (MV2, Munim, Inc.); not checked by a human mathematician
definition: K in F_3^n is a Kakeya set if for every nonzero direction d it contains a full line {a, a+d, a+2d}; k_n is the least size of a Kakeya set in F_3^n

7.structure: the layer x0 = 0 is exactly the 105-point set of F_3^6; layers x0 = 1 and 2 add 56 + 50 = 106 points, which is 2 * 53

8.structure: the layer x0 = 0 is exactly the 211-point set of F_3^7; layers x0 = 1 and 2 add 96 + 115 = 211 points, so the set has 2 * 211 points

9.structure: the layer x0 = 0 is exactly the 422-point set of F_3^8; layers x0 = 1 and 2 add 424 points, so the set has 2 * 422 + 2 points (the split of the 424 points between the two layers is reported by k8/probe10.py)

asymptotic_constructions: Kopparty, Lev, Saraf and Sudan (arXiv:1003.3736, Theorem 8) give Kakeya sets in F_3^n of size (3 / 2^(2/3))^(n + O(sqrt n)), base about 1.8899, by a random construction; it gives no explicit sets for small n

lev_pattern.source: V. F. Lev, comment 994 on T. Tao's blog, 14 March 2009: 'I am very curious to know whether k_5 = 53: notice the pattern in 3, 7, 13, 27, 53, ...'; Chung, Du and Wesley (arXiv:2608.23691) state it as the recurrence k_n = k_(n-1) + 2 k_(n-2) and say whether it continues remains open
lev_pattern.consequence: k_6 <= 105 < 107, k_7 <= 211 < 213, k_8 <= 422 < 427 and k_9 <= 846 < 853: our sets lie below the pattern in all four dimensions, by 2, 2, 5 and 7 points. Since k_2 = 7 and k_3 = 13, the recurrence cannot hold at all of n = 4, 5, 6: if it did, k_6 would be 107. With k_4 = 27 it fails at n = 5 or n = 6: either k_5 <= 52, or k_5 = 53 and k_6 <= 105 = k_5 + 2 k_4 - 2.

recurrence_on_true_values.note: if k_7 <= k_6 + 2 k_5 held, k_7 would be at most 105 + 2 * 53 = 211; the 211-point set reaches exactly this value, as a 105-point layer plus 106 = 2 * 53 points in the other two layers. The same reading in F_3^8 gives 211 + 2 * 105 = 421 and in F_3^9 gives 422 + 2 * 211 = 844. The 422-point set has a 211-point layer plus 211 points (one more than 421); the 846-point set has a 422-point layer plus 424 points (two more than 844).

layer_observation.note: A search that keeps a record Kakeya set A of F_3^(n-1) fixed in one layer needed |L1| + |L2| of: 27 in F_3^5 (on a 27-point layer), 54 in F_3^6 (on the 53-point layer), 106 in F_3^7 (on the 105-point layer), 211 in F_3^8 (on the 211-point layer; 10 runs of about 400 s not started from the 422-point set gave 211, 212, 212, 216, 216, 216, 220, 224, 227 and 390) and 424 in F_3^9 (on the 422-point layer, from the product start). So the extra cost was about the size of the layer itself, k_(n-1) to k_(n-1) + 2, which is also about 2 k_(n-2). This is an observation from stalled searches, not a theorem. The census of k8/CENSUS.md (F_3^5, 331 different 27- to 32-point layers) never went below 27 + 27 = 54, and in F_3^3 layered sets need at least 14 points (k8/CENSUS.md) while k_3 = 13.

Starts: '-' fresh (greedy), '422' the 422-point set's own layers, 'lift' L1 = F_3 x A, L2 = F_3 x B with A, B the free layers of the 422-point set (1055 points, Kakeya by construction), 'prod' L1 = L2 = the 422-point set (F_3 x K8, 1266 points). first_reached lists the last two (extra, seconds) entries. 'verified' is k8.check.is_kakeya on the full set (not run for n = 9 sets of 1023 points or more).

free_layer_comparison.note: A, B = the layers x0 = 1 and 2 of the 422-point set, K = its layer x0 = 0 (the 211-point set); the same for the 211-point set of F_3^7 (K = the 105-point set). |A u B| would have to be Kakeya for a simple recursion; it is not. Overlaps: max over t of |(A u B) cap (K + t)| and |(A u B) cap (-K + t)|, and max over t of |A cap (B + t)| and |A cap (-B + t)|.

search_log.note: first_reached lists (size, seconds) when each size was first reached; intermediate entries omitted. Every final set was re-checked by k5.walk.is_kakeya or k8.check.is_kakeya in the run, and the record sets are re-checked by k6/test_sets.py and k6/test_layers.py at every commit. 'structure' numbers were printed by k6/probe2.py stats() or k8/probe8.py line_stats(): lines = number of full lines in the set, single_line_directions = directions covered by exactly one line, removable_points = points whose removal keeps the set Kakeya, section_min/max = smallest and largest of the 3 x 364 (or 3 x 1093) hyperplane sections, K_cap_minus_K = |K intersect -K|.
